newsitem.title: USA: IRS to lift electronic pay requirement for some firms.
newsitem.headline: IRS to lift electronic pay requirement for some firms.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service will not require the smallest businesses to make tax payments electronically, a Treasury official said Thursday.
Businesses that deposited $20,000 in annual federal payroll taxes such as withholding and Social Security would have had to make those payments electronically in 1999.

However, the required target that 94 percent of all depository taxes be collected by electronic fund transfer is expected to be met by the end of 1998, said Donald Lubick, acting assistant Treasury secretary for tax policy.

So, the threshold for requiring electronic tax payments will stop at businesses that deposited more than $50,000 in annual federal payroll taxes. Those firms were required to begin electronic tax payments July 1.
"I am pleased to announce that we intend to amend the regulations within the next month to make the $50,000 threshold permanent," Lubick said in testimony at a Senate Finance subcommittee hearing.

The IRS this week deferred for six months imposing penalties on small businesses that did not make tax payments electronically as required. The penalty of 10 percent on tax deposits will not be imposed through Dec. 31 to give businesses another six months to comply with the requirement of paying taxes electronically by telephone or computer.
The penalty has been criticised by Congress members, who say it would hurt small businesses.

Sen. Don Nickles, Oklahoma Republican, has introduced legislation that would put the threshold for required electronic filing at $5 million annual payroll tax deposits and make it voluntary for smaller businesses to participate.
Nickles said at the hearing that electronic tax payments should be voluntary for small businesses. "I don't like the gun at their head," he said.
